sectionTitle: Identification of ions by chemical and spectroscopic means (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Flame tests can be used to identify some metal ions (cations). Lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper compounds produce distinctive colours in flame tests:
lithium compounds result in a crimson flame
sodium compounds result in a yellow flame
potassium compounds result in a lilac flame
calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame
copper compounds result in a green flame.
If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used some flame colours can be masked.
Students should be able to identify species from the results of the tests in 4.8.3.1 to 4.8.3.5.
Flame colours of other metal ions are not required knowledge.
Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions form white precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added but only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.
Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.
Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate, iron(II) a green precipitate and iron(III) a brown precipitate.
Students should be able to write balanced equations for the reactions to produce the insoluble hydroxides.
Students are not expected to write equations for the production of sodium aluminate.
Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas. Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater.
Halide ions in solution produce precipitates with silver nitrate solution in the presence of dilute nitric acid. Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
Sulfate ions in solution produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.
Required practical 7: use of chemical tests to identify the ions in unknown single ionic compounds covering the ions from sections Flame tests to Sulfates .
Elements and compounds can be detected and identified using instrumental methods. Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.
Students should be able to state advantages of instrumental methods compared with the chemical tests in this specification.
Flame emission spectroscopy is an example of an instrumental method used to analyse metal ions in solutions.

The sample is put into a flame and the light given out is passed through a spectroscope. The output is a line spectrum that can be analysed to identify the metal ions in the solution and measure their concentrations.

Students should be able to interpret an instrumental result given appropriate data in chart or tabular form, when accompanied by a reference set in the same form, limited to flame emission spectroscopy.

scopeNotes.statement: Flame colours of other metal ions are not required knowledge.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the five flame colours named in the specification are taught and assessed: lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red and copper green. Other metals in this section (aluminium, magnesium, iron(II), iron(III)) are identified only by their reactions with sodium hydroxide solution; no flame colour is stated for them and no question can be answered by knowing one.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not expected to write equations for the production of sodium aluminate.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The dissolving of aluminium hydroxide in excess sodium hydroxide solution is assessed only as an observation that distinguishes aluminium from calcium and magnesium. No item asks for, or accepts, an equation for the production of sodium aluminate; the only equations required are those for the insoluble hydroxides.

concepts.definition: A test in which a sample of a compound is held on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame; some metal ions colour the flame, and the colour identifies the metal ion.
A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses electrons. Metal ions are cations, and it is the cation that a flame test identifies.
The deep red flame colour produced by lithium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by sodium compounds in a flame test.
The pale purple flame colour produced by potassium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by calcium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by copper compounds in a flame test.
The hiding of one flame colour by another when a sample contains a mixture of ions; a strong colour such as the yellow of sodium can cover a weaker colour.
Naming the ions, and hence the compound, present in a sample by combining the results of the flame test, sodium hydroxide test, carbonate test, halide test and sulfate test.
Adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution of an unknown salt; metal ions that form insoluble hydroxides give precipitates whose colour identifies the metal ion.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed; here, an insoluble metal hydroxide formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added.
The white precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of aluminium, calcium or magnesium ions.
Adding more sodium hydroxide solution than is needed to precipitate the hydroxide; only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves, which distinguishes aluminium from calcium and magnesium.
The coloured precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of copper(II), iron(II) or iron(III) ions.
Cu(OH)2, the blue precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution containing copper(II) ions.
Fe(OH)2, the green precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution containing iron(II) ions.
Fe(OH)3, the brown precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution containing iron(III) ions.

concepts.term: Balanced equation for a hydroxide precipitate
concepts.definition: An equation such as FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl, in which the numbers of atoms of each element are the same on both sides.
Adding dilute acid to a carbonate; the carbonate fizzes and gives off carbon dioxide gas.
A solution of calcium hydroxide used to test for carbon dioxide; it turns milky (cloudy) when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it.
Adding dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution to a solution; a precipitate of the silver halide forms, and its colour identifies the halide ion.
Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
Adding dilute hydrochloric acid and then barium chloride solution to a solution; a white precipitate of barium sulfate shows that sulfate ions are present.
The practical in which chemical tests are used to identify the ions in unknown single ionic compounds, covering the ions from flame tests through to sulfates.
A method of detecting and identifying elements and compounds using a machine rather than a chemical test.
The three advantages of instrumental methods: they give results close to the true value, they can detect very small amounts, and they work quickly.
An instrumental method used to analyse metal ions in solutions, both to identify them and to measure their concentrations.
The instrument through which the light given out by the sample in the flame is passed, producing a line spectrum.
The output of flame emission spectroscopy: a pattern of lines that can be analysed to identify the metal ions present and to measure their concentrations.
A set of known line spectra, in the same chart or table form as the sample result, against which the sample's lines are compared to identify its metal ions.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do sodium compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Sodium compounds result in a yellow flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Sodium gives an orange flame, because sodium street lamps glow orange.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium street lamps and burning sodium both look orange to the eye, and the orange-red of calcium sits next to sodium in the list of colours.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is exact: sodium compounds result in a yellow flame; the orange-red flame belongs to calcium.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do lithium compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Lithium compounds result in a crimson flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Lithium gives a lilac flame because all Group 1 metals behave the same way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that Group 1 metals have similar chemical reactions and wrongly extend this to flame colour, so lithium is given potassium's lilac.
misconceptions.correction: Flame colour is specific to each metal ion: lithium is crimson, sodium yellow and potassium lilac, even though all three are in Group 1.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do potassium compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Potassium compounds result in a lilac flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Potassium gives a yellow flame like sodium, as both are Group 1 metals.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium impurities in glassware and in samples often make a yellow colour appear during any flame test, which reinforces the idea that Group 1 means yellow.
misconceptions.correction: Potassium compounds result in a lilac flame; a yellow colour indicates sodium, which may be present as an impurity.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do calcium compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Calcium gives a crimson flame.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Crimson and orange-red are both reddish, so the lithium and calcium colours are easily swapped when they are memorised as one 'red' group.
misconceptions.correction: Lithium is crimson (a deep red); calcium is orange-red. The specification names the two colours separately because they identify different ions.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do copper compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Copper compounds result in a green flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper gives a blue flame, because copper sulfate solution and copper(II) hydroxide are blue.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper is strongly associated with blue from copper(II) compounds, so the flame colour is predicted from the colour of the solid or solution.
misconceptions.correction: The colour of a copper compound is not its flame colour: copper compounds result in a green flame.

misconceptions.question: What does the colour of a flame test identify?
misconceptions.correct: It identifies the metal ion (cation) in the compound.
misconceptions.misconception: The flame colour identifies the negative ion (anion) in the compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The compound's name ends with the non-metal part, so students read the test as a test on the second half of the name.
misconceptions.correction: Flame tests identify metal ions (cations). Anions such as chloride, carbonate and sulfate are found using other tests.

misconceptions.question: Does a flame test identify a compound or an ion?
misconceptions.correct: It identifies the metal ion present, not the whole compound.
misconceptions.misconception: The flame colour identifies the whole compound, so every sodium compound would need its own colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think in terms of substances rather than ions, so the observation is attached to the compound as a whole.
misconceptions.correction: All sodium compounds give the same yellow flame because the colour comes from the sodium ion; the flame test names the metal ion only.

misconceptions.question: What is seen when a mixture of metal ions is used in a flame test?
misconceptions.correct: Some flame colours can be masked by others.
misconceptions.misconception: Every ion in the mixture shows its own colour, so all the colours are seen at once.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume observations simply add together, as they do when solids are mixed, rather than one bright colour swamping another.
misconceptions.correction: If a sample contains a mixture of ions, some flame colours can be masked; a strong colour such as sodium's yellow can hide a weaker one.

misconceptions.question: A crimson flame is not seen from a mixture containing lithium ions. Why?
misconceptions.correct: The lithium colour has been masked by another, stronger colour.
misconceptions.misconception: The lithium ions must have been destroyed or used up in the flame.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Not seen' is read as 'not there', and burning is associated with substances being destroyed.
misconceptions.correction: Masking hides a colour but does not remove the ion; the lithium ions are still present and would be found by another method.

misconceptions.question: How is the sodium hydroxide test carried out?
misconceptions.correct: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of the unknown compound.
misconceptions.misconception: Solid sodium hydroxide is added to the dry solid compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The test is remembered as 'add sodium hydroxide' without the requirement for both to be in solution, which is what allows a precipitate to form.
misconceptions.correction: Both must be in solution: a precipitate is an insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed.

misconceptions.question: Which white hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution?
misconceptions.correct: Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves.
misconceptions.misconception: All three white precipitates dissolve if enough sodium hydroxide solution is added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students generalise from 'excess reagent dissolves the solid' and treat the three white precipitates as chemically identical because they look the same.
misconceptions.correction: Aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions all give white precipitates, but only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.

misconceptions.question: Does calcium hydroxide dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide solution?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess.
misconceptions.misconception: Calcium hydroxide dissolves, because limewater is a solution of calcium hydroxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Limewater shows that calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble, so students conclude that the precipitate will redissolve.
misconceptions.correction: The white precipitate that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution is aluminium hydroxide; the calcium and magnesium precipitates remain.

misconceptions.question: Which ions give white precipitates with sodium hydroxide solution?
misconceptions.correct: Aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions give white precipitates.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnesium ions give a coloured precipitate, like the transition metal ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Magnesium is a metal that forms a hydroxide, and students who have just met the coloured precipitates apply them too widely.
misconceptions.correction: The coloured precipitates come from copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) only. Aluminium, calcium and magnesium give white precipitates.

misconceptions.question: What colours are the iron hydroxide precipitates?
misconceptions.correct: Iron(II) gives a green precipitate and iron(III) a brown precipitate.
misconceptions.misconception: Iron(II) gives a brown precipitate and iron(III) a green one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two iron ions are easily confused, and rust (iron(III)) being brown is not always connected to the (III) label.
misconceptions.correction: Iron(II) hydroxide is green; iron(III) hydroxide is brown. The higher charge goes with the brown precipitate.

misconceptions.question: What colour is the copper(II) hydroxide precipitate?
misconceptions.correct: Copper(II) hydroxide is a blue precipitate.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper(II) hydroxide is green, because copper roofs and copper carbonate are green.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Green is strongly linked to copper through verdigris and copper carbonate, and green is also the copper flame colour.
misconceptions.correction: With sodium hydroxide solution, copper(II) gives a blue precipitate; the green precipitate is iron(II) hydroxide.

misconceptions.question: Where does the colour of the precipitate come from?
misconceptions.correct: It comes from the metal ion that has been precipitated.
misconceptions.misconception: The colour comes from the sodium hydroxide solution that was added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The sodium hydroxide is the thing being added, so students attribute the new observation to it.
misconceptions.correction: Sodium hydroxide solution is colourless. The colour identifies the metal ion in the insoluble hydroxide formed.

misconceptions.question: How is the equation for the hydroxide precipitate balanced?
misconceptions.correct: FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl
misconceptions.misconception: FeCl3 + NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + NaCl, with no balancing numbers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students write the formulae correctly and then stop, without checking that the numbers of sodium and chlorine atoms match on both sides.
misconceptions.correction: An iron(III) ion needs three hydroxide ions, so three NaOH are required and three NaCl are produced.

misconceptions.question: What is the formula of the precipitate formed from iron(III) ions?
misconceptions.correct: Fe(OH)3
misconceptions.misconception: Fe(OH)2, the same formula as for iron(II).
misconceptions.whyItArises: The charge on the metal ion is not carried through into the formula, and Fe(OH)2 is the more familiar-looking formula.
misconceptions.correction: Iron(III) ions are Fe3+, so three hydroxide ions are needed and the precipitate is Fe(OH)3.

misconceptions.question: Which gas is given off when a carbonate reacts with a dilute acid?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide is given off.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen is given off, because an acid is reacting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reaction of an acid with a metal, which gives hydrogen, is the more familiar reaction and fizzing is associated with hydrogen.
misconceptions.correction: Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas; metals, not carbonates, give hydrogen with acids.

misconceptions.question: What happens to limewater when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it?
misconceptions.correct: The limewater turns milky (cloudy).
misconceptions.misconception: The limewater changes colour, for example turning blue, because carbon dioxide is acidic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gas tests are remembered as colour changes because indicators are the more familiar way of detecting an acid.
misconceptions.correction: Limewater goes milky because insoluble calcium carbonate forms; it is a precipitate, not an indicator colour change.

misconceptions.question: How is carbon dioxide identified?
misconceptions.correct: It turns limewater milky.
misconceptions.misconception: It relights a glowing splint.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three common gas tests are learned as a set and the splint tests are swapped with the limewater test.
misconceptions.correction: A glowing splint relighting shows oxygen. Carbon dioxide is identified with limewater, which turns milky.

misconceptions.question: What colour are the silver halide precipitates?
misconceptions.correct: Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
misconceptions.misconception: Silver bromide is yellow and silver iodide is cream.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cream and yellow are close in appearance, and the order of the halogens is not linked to the order of the colours.
misconceptions.correction: The colours deepen down the group: chloride white, bromide cream, iodide yellow.

misconceptions.question: Which acid is used when testing for halide ions?
misconceptions.correct: Dilute nitric acid is used with silver nitrate solution.
misconceptions.misconception: Dilute hydrochloric acid is used, as in the sulfate test.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dilute hydrochloric acid is the acid used in the sulfate test, so it is carried over into the halide test.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions, which would give a white precipitate with silver nitrate whatever the sample was. Dilute nitric acid is used instead.

misconceptions.question: Which reagents are used to test for sulfate ions?
misconceptions.correct: Dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride solution.
misconceptions.misconception: Dilute sulfuric acid and barium chloride solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sulfuric acid is the acid whose name matches 'sulfate', so it is chosen by name rather than by chemistry.
misconceptions.correction: Sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions and would give a white precipitate every time. The sulfate test uses dilute hydrochloric acid.

misconceptions.question: What is seen when barium chloride solution is added to a sulfate solution?
misconceptions.correct: A white precipitate of barium sulfate forms.
misconceptions.misconception: A cream precipitate forms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The precipitate colours from the halide test are transferred to the sulfate test because both produce precipitates.
misconceptions.correction: Sulfate ions in solution produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.

misconceptions.question: How do instrumental methods compare with chemical tests for speed?
misconceptions.correct: Instrumental methods are rapid.
misconceptions.misconception: Instrumental methods are slower, because the machine has to be set up and calibrated.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Laboratory experience of waiting for equipment makes machines seem slow compared with a quick test-tube test.
misconceptions.correction: Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid; that speed is one of their advantages over chemical tests.

misconceptions.question: How much substance do instrumental methods need?
misconceptions.correct: They are sensitive, so they can detect very small amounts.
misconceptions.misconception: They need a larger sample than a chemical test because the machine is large.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The size of the instrument is confused with the size of the sample it needs.
misconceptions.correction: Instrumental methods are sensitive: they detect and identify very small amounts of a substance, smaller than a chemical test could find.

misconceptions.question: What can flame emission spectroscopy analyse?
misconceptions.correct: It analyses metal ions in solutions.
misconceptions.misconception: It identifies any ion, including halide and sulfate ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Having replaced several chemical tests with one machine, students assume the machine does everything the tests did.
misconceptions.correction: Flame emission spectroscopy is used to analyse metal ions in solutions; the specification limits it to that.

misconceptions.question: What can a line spectrum tell you?
misconceptions.correct: It identifies the metal ions present and measures their concentrations.
misconceptions.misconception: It only tells you which metal ions are present, not how much of them there is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The test is learned as an identification test, so the quantitative part of the output is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: The line spectrum can be analysed both to identify the metal ions in the solution and to measure their concentrations.

misconceptions.question: What is the output of flame emission spectroscopy?
misconceptions.correct: A line spectrum.
misconceptions.misconception: A continuous spectrum, like the one made when white light passes through a prism.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Splitting light is associated with the rainbow spectrum met in physics, so the same output is expected here.
misconceptions.correction: The light given out by the sample is passed through a spectroscope and the output is a line spectrum.

misconceptions.question: How is a sample's line spectrum used with a reference set?
misconceptions.correct: The positions of the sample's lines are matched against the reference spectra.
misconceptions.misconception: The metal with the largest number of lines in the reference set is the one present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Counting lines is easier than comparing their positions, so a tally replaces the comparison.
misconceptions.correction: A metal ion is present only if the lines in its reference spectrum appear in the sample's spectrum, at the same positions.

misconceptions.question: How is an unknown single ionic compound identified in Required practical 7?
misconceptions.correct: A test for the metal ion and a test for the non-metal ion are both needed.
misconceptions.misconception: One positive test is enough to name the compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Each test is taught as 'the test for X', so a single result feels like a complete answer.
misconceptions.correction: An ionic compound contains a cation and an anion, so tests for both are needed before it can be named.

misconceptions.question: Why must the wire be cleaned between flame tests?
misconceptions.correct: Any compound left on the wire would give its own colour and mask or add to the next result.
misconceptions.misconception: Cleaning the wire only matters because the wire itself would burn.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The cleaning step is remembered as equipment care rather than as a way of preventing a false result.
misconceptions.correction: A trace of a previous sample, especially a sodium compound, gives a strong colour that can mask the colour of the sample being tested.

mcqs.stem: A student holds a sample of an unknown ionic compound in a hot Bunsen flame and a strong colour appears. What does the flame colour identify?

options.text: the metal ion (cation) present in the compound
options.rationale: Flame tests can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

options.text: the non-metal ion (anion) that it contains
options.rationale: Students who read the second half of the compound's name expect the test to name the negative ion.

options.text: the compound as a whole, not just one ion
options.rationale: Thinking in substances rather than ions makes the colour a property of the compound.

options.text: the temperature reached by the hot flame
options.rationale: Flame colour is linked to heat in everyday life, so temperature is a tempting reading.

mcqs.stem: A clean wire is dipped in a lithium compound and held in a blue Bunsen flame. What is seen?

options.text: a lilac flame, as for Group 1 metals
options.rationale: Group 1 metals react similarly, so their flame colours are wrongly assumed to match.

options.text: a crimson flame, a strong deep red
options.rationale: Lithium compounds result in a crimson flame.

options.text: an orange-red flame, as calcium gives
options.rationale: Crimson and orange-red are both reddish and are readily swapped.

options.text: a yellow flame that fades fast
options.rationale: Sodium impurities often add yellow, which students take to be the lithium colour.

mcqs.stem: Which flame colour does the specification give for sodium compounds?

options.text: orange, like a sodium street lamp
options.rationale: Sodium street lamps glow orange, which overrides the specification's colour.

options.text: orange-red, a deep reddish shade
options.rationale: The calcium colour is taken for sodium because both are read as 'orange'.

options.text: yellow, a bright clear yellow
options.rationale: Sodium compounds result in a yellow flame.

options.text: lilac, a pale purple colour
options.rationale: Sodium and potassium are both Group 1, so their colours are interchanged.

mcqs.stem: Which flame colour identifies potassium compounds?

options.text: yellow, the colour sodium gives
options.rationale: Sodium impurities make yellow appear in many flame tests, reinforcing the error.

options.text: crimson, the colour lithium gives
options.rationale: All three metals are in Group 1, so their colours are treated as one.

options.text: green, the colour copper gives
options.rationale: Copper's green is the least familiar colour and is often mis-assigned.

options.text: lilac, a pale purple colour
options.rationale: Potassium compounds result in a lilac flame.

mcqs.stem: A compound gives an orange-red flame in a flame test. Which metal ion does it contain?

options.text: lithium ions, a strong crimson flame
options.rationale: Crimson is read as an orange-red, so lithium is chosen.

options.text: calcium ions, an orange-red flame
options.rationale: Calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame.

options.text: sodium ions, a bright yellow flame
options.rationale: Sodium is remembered as orange, so an orange-red flame is read as sodium.

options.text: copper ions, a light green flame
options.rationale: Copper is chosen when the colour is not securely known.

mcqs.stem: Which flame colour do copper compounds give?

options.text: blue, the colour of copper sulfate
options.rationale: The blue of copper(II) compounds is transferred to the flame.

options.text: lilac, the pale purple colour
options.rationale: Lilac is the least used colour and is assigned to the least familiar metal.

options.text: green, a distinctive green flame
options.rationale: Copper compounds result in a green flame.

options.text: yellow, a bright yellow colour
options.rationale: Yellow is the colour most often seen in practice, from sodium impurities.

mcqs.stem: A solution contains both sodium ions and lithium ions. In a flame test only a yellow flame is seen. Why is no crimson flame seen?

options.text: both colours appear, but only one at a time
options.rationale: Observations are assumed to add together rather than one hiding another.

options.text: the lithium ions were destroyed by heating
options.rationale: 'Not seen' is read as 'not there', and burning suggests destruction.

options.text: the two colours have mixed to yellow
options.rationale: Colour mixing from art is applied to the flame test.

options.text: the yellow colour has masked the crimson
options.rationale: If a sample contains a mixture of ions some flame colours can be masked.

mcqs.stem: Why must the wire be cleaned in acid between flame tests?

options.text: so that a trace of the last sample cannot mask the next colour
options.rationale: A leftover compound gives its own colour, which can mask the sample's colour.

options.text: so that the ions in the sample are not destroyed by the flame
options.rationale: Masking is confused with the ion being used up.

options.text: so that every ion present shows its own separate colour
options.rationale: Students expect all colours to be visible at once.

options.text: so that the wire itself does not burn away in the hot flame
options.rationale: The step is read as equipment care rather than avoiding a false result.

mcqs.stem: An unknown compound gives a lilac flame. Adding silver nitrate solution and dilute nitric acid gives a cream precipitate. What is the compound?

options.text: potassium chloride, KCl
options.rationale: Cream is read as white, so chloride is chosen.

options.text: lithium bromide, LiBr
options.rationale: Lilac is assigned to lithium when Group 1 colours are merged.

options.text: potassium bromide, KBr
options.rationale: Lilac shows potassium; a cream silver halide precipitate shows bromide.

options.text: potassium iodide, KI
options.rationale: Cream and yellow are swapped, so the iodide is chosen instead.

mcqs.stem: A solution gives a green precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution, and a white precipitate with dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride solution. What is the compound?

options.text: iron(III) sulfate, Fe2(SO4)3
options.rationale: The two iron ions are swapped, so green is read as iron(III).

options.text: copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4
options.rationale: Copper is linked to green through copper carbonate and its flame colour.

options.text: iron(II) chloride, FeCl2
options.rationale: The white precipitate is credited to the hydrochloric acid rather than to sulfate.

options.text: iron(II) sulfate, FeSO4
options.rationale: A green hydroxide precipitate shows iron(II); the white precipitate with barium chloride shows sulfate.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of an unknown salt. What is this test for?

options.text: the metal ion, by its precipitate
options.rationale: Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

options.text: the negative ion, shown by the colour
options.rationale: The idea that a test names the second half of the compound persists.

options.text: the acid left over in the solution
options.rationale: Sodium hydroxide is met first as a neutralising alkali.

options.text: the sodium ions in the solution
options.rationale: The reagent added is assumed to be what is detected.

mcqs.stem: Why must the unknown compound be dissolved in water before sodium hydroxide is added?

options.text: so that the solid does not react too violently with it
options.rationale: Dissolving is seen as a way of diluting a dangerous reaction.

options.text: so that two solutions mix and a precipitate forms
options.rationale: A precipitate is an insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed.

options.text: so that the metal ions can be made in the water
options.rationale: Ions are thought to be created by dissolving rather than separated.

options.text: so that the dry solid can be weighed out first
options.rationale: The step is read as a measuring step, not a chemical requirement.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to separate solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions. What is seen?

options.text: a coloured precipitate in every tube
options.rationale: The coloured precipitates are applied to all metal ions.

options.text: a white precipitate with calcium only
options.rationale: Only the most familiar metal is expected to react.

options.text: no precipitate with aluminium ions
options.rationale: Aluminium's dissolving in excess is remembered as no precipitate at all.

options.text: a white precipitate forms in every tube
options.rationale: Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions form white precipitates.

mcqs.stem: Excess sodium hydroxide solution is added to the three white precipitates. Which precipitate dissolves?

options.text: the aluminium hydroxide
options.rationale: Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.

options.text: the calcium hydroxide only
options.rationale: Limewater being a solution of calcium hydroxide suggests it redissolves.

options.text: all three of the hydroxides
options.rationale: Excess reagent is assumed to dissolve any precipitate.

options.text: the magnesium hydroxide only
options.rationale: One precipitate is known to dissolve, and the wrong one is chosen.

mcqs.stem: Which set of ions forms coloured precipitates with sodium hydroxide solution?

options.text: aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions
options.rationale: The white precipitate ions are chosen instead.

options.text: copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III)
options.rationale: Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured precipitates.

options.text: iron(II), calcium and magnesium ions
options.rationale: One coloured ion is mixed in with white precipitate ions.

options.text: lithium, sodium and calcium ions
options.rationale: Group 1 and calcium ions are picked, with the colour credited to the added alkali.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is colourless, yet the precipitate it forms is coloured. Where does the colour come from?

options.text: from the sodium in the sodium hydroxide
options.rationale: The reagent added is credited with the new observation.

options.text: from the hydroxide ions in the alkali
options.rationale: The other half of the reagent is credited instead.

options.text: from the metal ion in the insoluble hydroxide
options.rationale: The colour identifies the metal ion that has been precipitated.

options.text: from the water the salt was dissolved in
options.rationale: The solvent is the remaining component and is chosen by elimination.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. What is seen?

options.text: a blue precipitate is formed
options.rationale: Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate.

options.text: a green precipitate is formed
options.rationale: Copper is linked to green through copper carbonate and its flame colour.

options.text: a brown precipitate forms
options.rationale: The three coloured precipitates are assigned at random when not learned.

options.text: a white precipitate is seen
options.rationale: The white precipitates are treated as the general case.

mcqs.stem: Two tubes contain iron salts. Sodium hydroxide solution gives a green precipitate in one and a brown precipitate in the other. What does this show?

options.text: green must be iron(III) and brown iron(II)
options.rationale: The two iron ions are swapped.

options.text: green is iron(II), brown is iron(III)
options.rationale: Iron(II) gives a green precipitate and iron(III) a brown precipitate.

options.text: green is copper(II), brown is iron(III)
options.rationale: Green is credited to copper.

options.text: green shows iron(II) and brown copper(II)
options.rationale: The unfamiliar brown is credited to copper.

mcqs.stem: Which balanced equation shows iron(III) chloride solution reacting with sodium hydroxide solution?

options.text: FeSO4 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4
options.rationale: The iron(II) reaction is written instead, giving Fe(OH)2.

options.text: FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + NaCl
options.rationale: The left side is balanced but the sodium and chlorine on the right are not.

options.text: FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl
options.rationale: Three hydroxide ions are needed for each Fe3+, so 3NaOH and 3NaCl balance the equation.

options.text: FeCl3 + NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + NaCl
options.rationale: Correct formulae are written and no balancing numbers are added.

mcqs.stem: Which balanced equation shows magnesium chloride solution reacting with sodium hydroxide solution?

options.text: MgCl2 + 2NaOH -> Mg(OH)2 + NaCl
options.rationale: The chlorine atoms are left unbalanced on the right.

options.text: MgCl2 + NaOH -> Mg(OH)2 + NaCl
options.rationale: No balancing numbers are added at all.

options.text: MgCl2 + KOH -> Mg(OH)2 + KCl
options.rationale: The wrong alkali is written in, and the equation is also left unbalanced.

options.text: MgCl2 + 2NaOH -> Mg(OH)2 + 2NaCl
options.rationale: Two hydroxide ions are needed for each Mg2+, so 2NaOH and 2NaCl balance the equation.

mcqs.stem: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a solid carbonate and the mixture fizzes. Which gas is given off?

options.text: hydrogen, because an acid is reacting
options.rationale: Acid plus metal giving hydrogen is the more familiar reaction.

options.text: carbon dioxide, from the carbonate
options.rationale: Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas.

options.text: chlorine, from the hydrochloric acid
options.rationale: The gas is predicted from the name of the acid used.

options.text: oxygen, released from the carbonate
options.rationale: The oxygen atoms in the carbonate ion suggest oxygen gas.

mcqs.stem: The gas given off by a carbonate is bubbled through limewater. What confirms it is carbon dioxide?

options.text: the limewater turns a pale blue
options.rationale: Gas tests are remembered as indicator colour changes.

options.text: a glowing splint would relight
options.rationale: The oxygen test is used by mistake.

options.text: the limewater turns milky
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater, which turns milky.

options.text: a lit splint would pop loudly
options.rationale: The hydrogen test is used by mistake.

mcqs.stem: Silver nitrate solution and dilute nitric acid are added to three halide solutions. Which result is correct?

options.text: the bromide gives a yellow precipitate
options.rationale: Cream and yellow are close in appearance, so the bromide is given the iodide's colour.

options.text: the chloride gives a yellow precipitate
options.rationale: The three colours are learned as a set but are not matched to the right halide.

options.text: all three of them give white precipitates
options.rationale: The white of silver chloride is generalised to every silver halide.

options.text: the bromide gives a cream precipitate
options.rationale: Silver bromide is cream; silver chloride is white and silver iodide is yellow.

mcqs.stem: Why is dilute nitric acid, and not dilute hydrochloric acid, used in the test for halide ions?

options.text: hydrochloric acid would add chloride ions to the sample
options.rationale: Chloride ions from the acid would give a white precipitate with silver nitrate whatever the sample was.

options.text: hydrochloric acid is far too weak to acidify the solution
options.rationale: The choice is put down to acid strength rather than to the ions present.

options.text: nitric acid makes the precipitate form much faster
options.rationale: The acid is thought to speed the reaction up.

options.text: nitric acid dissolves the silver nitrate solid
options.rationale: The acid is thought to be a solvent for the reagent.

mcqs.stem: Which reagents are used to test a solution for sulfate ions, and what is seen?

options.text: dilute hydrochloric acid and silver nitrate; a cream precipitate
options.rationale: The halide test reagents and colours are used instead.

options.text: dilute sulfuric acid and barium chloride; a white precipitate
options.rationale: The acid is chosen because its name matches the ion being tested for.

options.text: dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride; a white precipitate
options.rationale: Sulfate ions produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.

options.text: dilute nitric acid and barium chloride; a cream precipitate
options.rationale: The acid from the halide test is carried over, with its colours.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 7 a student must identify both ions in an unknown single ionic compound. Which plan is correct?

options.text: do a flame test only, and name the compound
options.rationale: One positive result feels like a complete identification.

options.text: add barium chloride first, and then silver nitrate
options.rationale: The chloride ions added with the first reagent would give a false positive.

options.text: add sodium hydroxide, then do a second flame test
options.rationale: Two cation tests are run and the anion is never tested for.

options.text: do a flame test, then test for the negative ion
options.rationale: An ionic compound contains a cation and an anion, so tests for both are needed.

mcqs.stem: What are instrumental methods used for, and what are they like?

options.text: detecting and identifying substances; they are accurate, sensitive and rapid
options.rationale: Elements and compounds can be detected and identified using instrumental methods, which are accurate, sensitive and rapid.

options.text: detecting and identifying substances; they are accurate but slow to use
options.rationale: Setting up and calibrating a machine makes it seem slow.

options.text: measuring temperature only; they are accurate, cheap and rapid
options.rationale: The instrument is thought to measure a physical quantity, not identity.

options.text: detecting substances only; they need quite a large sample of it
options.rationale: The size of the machine is confused with the size of the sample.

mcqs.stem: Give an advantage of using an instrumental method rather than a chemical test.

options.text: it takes much longer, so the result is always reliable
options.rationale: Slowness is equated with care and reliability.

options.text: it can detect a much smaller amount of the substance
options.rationale: Instrumental methods are sensitive, so tiny amounts are detected.

options.text: it does not need the sample to be pure at all
options.rationale: Sensitivity is confused with tolerance of impurities.

options.text: it works without any sample of the substance
options.rationale: Sensitivity is exaggerated into needing nothing.

mcqs.stem: What is flame emission spectroscopy used to analyse?

options.text: halide ions in solutions
options.rationale: The machine is assumed to replace every chemical test.

options.text: gases given off by solids
options.rationale: The flame suggests a test on a gas.

options.text: all ions in a solid sample
options.rationale: The requirement for a solution is dropped.

options.text: metal ions in solutions
options.rationale: Flame emission spectroscopy is an instrumental method used to analyse metal ions in solutions.

mcqs.stem: In flame emission spectroscopy, what happens to the light given out by the sample?

options.text: it is passed through a spectroscope
options.rationale: The sample is put into a flame and the light given out is passed through a spectroscope.

options.text: it is passed through a coloured filter
options.rationale: A filter is a more familiar way of separating colours.

options.text: it is reflected from a bright screen
options.rationale: The instrument is assumed to measure temperature.

options.text: it is measured with a thermometer
options.rationale: Optics from physics is imported without the spectroscope.

mcqs.stem: What can the output of flame emission spectroscopy be used for?

options.text: identifying which metal ions are there but not how much of them
options.rationale: The method is remembered only as an identification test.

options.text: identifying the metal ions and measuring their concentrations
options.rationale: The line spectrum can be analysed to identify the metal ions and measure their concentrations.

options.text: measuring concentration but not identifying which ion it is
options.rationale: The quantitative output is taken to be the only output.

options.text: identifying the compound rather than the ions it contains
options.rationale: Thinking in substances rather than ions carries over from flame tests.

mcqs.stem: A sample's line spectrum is compared with a reference set of spectra in the same form. How is a metal ion identified?

options.text: its reference spectrum has more lines in it than the other references
options.rationale: Counting lines is easier than comparing their positions.

options.text: its reference lines are brighter than the matching lines in the sample
options.rationale: Line intensity is used as the identifier instead of position.

options.text: its reference lines all appear in the sample spectrum, at the same positions
options.rationale: A metal ion is present when the lines of its reference spectrum match the sample's lines.

options.text: its reference spectrum covers the same overall range as the sample
options.rationale: A rough overall match replaces a line-by-line comparison.
